```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 5
)
library(TSP)
```

This vignette shows how to use the R package **TSP** [@Hahsler+Hornik2007]
for rearrangement clustering.
Solving a TSP can be used to cluster objects and to find a linear order of
objects. This was suggested several times in the literature
[@Lenstra1974; @Alpert1997; @Johnson2004]. The idea is that objects in the same
cluster are visited consecutively, so a short tour through all objects only
makes a large "jump" when it moves from one cluster to the next.

@Climer2006 call this approach *rearrangement clustering* and show how the
cluster boundaries can be found automatically: to obtain $k$ clusters, add $k$
*dummy cities* that have the same constant distance to all other cities and are
infinitely far from each other. In an optimal tour, the dummy cities must
separate the most distant groups of cities and thus represent the cluster
boundaries.

In **TSP**, dummy cities are added with `insert_dummy()` and the tour is split
into paths (clusters) with `cut_tour()`.

## Preparing the problem

We use the iris data, which contains measurements for 150 flowers of three
species. Since we know the species, we can check how well the clustering
recovers them. We create a TSP from the Euclidean distances between the
measurements and use the species as city labels.

```{r problem}
data("iris")
x <- iris[, 1:4]

tsp <- TSP(dist(x), labels = iris$Species)
tsp
```

Now we add three dummy cities labeled `"boundary"`.

```{r dummy}
tsp_dummy <- insert_dummy(tsp, n = 3, label = "boundary")
tsp_dummy
```

The default constant distance of 0 is guaranteed to work if the solver finds the
optimal tour. For heuristics, which are not optimal, a larger `const` (e.g.,
`2 * max(tsp)`) may give better results.

## Solving

We solve the problem with the default heuristic. Since the heuristic is not
optimal, it is not guaranteed that the dummy cities represent the best cluster
boundaries.

```{r solve}
tour <- solve_TSP(tsp_dummy, rep = 10, seed = 100)
tour
```

## Visualizing the result

The permuted distance matrix shows the clusters as dark blocks along the
diagonal. Light areas represent large distances. The red lines mark the
positions of the dummy cities in the tour, i.e., the cluster boundaries.

```{r image, fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
image(tsp_dummy, tour, xlab = "objects", ylab = "objects")

boundaries <- which(labels(tour) == "boundary")
abline(h = boundaries, col = "red")
abline(v = boundaries, col = "red")
```

## Extracting the clusters

`cut_tour()` cuts the tour at the dummy cities and returns the paths between
them. Each path is a cluster. Here, we get a list of index vectors into the
original data (the dummy cities are excluded).

```{r cut}
clusters <- cut_tour(tour, cut = "boundary")
lengths(clusters)
```

Because the tour is a cycle, the part of the tour after the last dummy city is
connected to the beginning of the tour, and `cut_tour()` takes care of this.
The cluster assignment can be converted into a label vector and compared to
the known species.

```{r labels}
# indices are positions in the data without dummy cities
cl <- integer(nrow(x))
for (i in seq_along(clusters)) cl[clusters[[i]]] <- i

table(cluster = cl, species = iris$Species)
```

With the seed used here, the three dummy cities split the data into groups of
40, 10 and 100 flowers. One boundary separates *Setosa* perfectly from the other
two species, but the second boundary only splits *Setosa* into two parts, while
*Versicolor* and *Virginica* end up in the same cluster. The exact result
depends on the heuristic and the seed, but the underlying reason is that
*Versicolor* and *Virginica* are close to each other in the feature space. This
problem is similar to the *chaining effect* in single-linkage hierarchical
clustering since the tour only uses the distances between neighboring points.

## Projecting the paths

To see the problem, we project the data on the first two principal components
and draw the paths that form the clusters.

```{r pca, fig.height=5}
pc <- prcomp(x)$x[, 1:2]
true_class <- as.integer(iris$Species)

plot(pc, pch = true_class, col = cl, xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")
for (p in clusters) lines(pc[p, ], col = "gray")
legend("topright", legend = levels(iris$Species), pch = 1:3)
```

The points of *Versicolor* and *Virginica* overlap, so it separates a few point
on the top side of the cluster.

## Ordering objects

If only a linear order of objects is needed (seriation) and not a clustering, a
single dummy city is enough to turn the tour into a path. The shortest path
through the distances is found by cutting the tour at the dummy city.

```{r seriation}
tsp1 <- insert_dummy(tsp, label = "cut")
tour1 <- solve_TSP(tsp1, seed = 1234)
path <- cut_tour(tour1, "cut")
head(path)
```

Reordering the distance matrix by this path groups similar objects together.

```{r seriation-image, fig.height=6, fig.width=6}
image(tsp, order = path)
```

The R package **seriation** [@Hahsler+Buchta+Hornik:2006] uses the TSP solvers
from **TSP** for seriation of general proximity matrices.
